title: Montepulciano
description: Central Italy's generous red grape, deep in colour and soft in tannin, from Abruzzo to the Marche.
L: Avoid the confusion with the Tuscan town

Montepulciano gives deep-coloured reds with ripe black cherry, plum, blackberry and dried herbs, sometimes liquorice. Tannins are plentiful but soft and ripe, acidity moderate. It's one of Italy's most planted red grapes and often offers good value.
Black cherry, soft tannin, deep colour

Montepulciano the grape has nothing to do with Montepulciano the Tuscan town, which makes Vino Nobile di Montepulciano from Sangiovese. The grape is grown mainly on the Adriatic side of central Italy. The confusion is so common that it's worth remembering: grape plus region, as in Montepulciano d'Abruzzo.
Grape in Abruzzo; town in Tuscany
What is Vino Nobile di Montepulciano made from?
Vino Nobile is a Tuscan wine made mainly from Sangiovese, named after the town.

Look for deep purple-ruby colour, ripe dark fruit and a soft, round texture with plenty of gentle tannin. It's less acidic than Sangiovese, rounder than Aglianico. A slightly bitter, herbal finish is common.
Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is made in the Tuscan town of Montepulciano.
Not true. It's made from the Montepulciano grape in Abruzzo, on the Adriatic coast.
Montepulciano gives deep, ripe, soft reds
The grape is unrelated to the Tuscan town
It's rounder and less acidic than Sangiovese

Montepulciano dominates Abruzzo, between the Apennines and the Adriatic. It's also important in the Marche, Molise and Puglia. In Abruzzo, the hills between mountains and sea give warm days and cool breezes. Vines are often trained on high pergolas, called tendone, which shade the fruit.

Montepulciano ripens late and needs warmth; in cooler years it can taste green and harsh. That's why it's rarely grown further north. Its thick skins give deep colour and resist disease. High yields are possible, so quality depends on controlling them.

In Abruzzo, look for Colline Teramane, a DOCG zone in the north of the region, for more structured Montepulciano.

Describe Montepulciano d'Abruzzo and its DOCG

Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC is huge, from cheap and cheerful to serious. Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane became DOCG in 2003, requiring at least 90% Montepulciano and longer ageing. Producers like Valentini and Emidio Pepe have shown how long-lived it can be.

Monte Conero is a limestone headland on the Adriatic, near Ancona in the Marche. Rosso Cònero DOC must be at least 85% Montepulciano. Conero DOCG, the Riserva, since 2004, requires two years of ageing. Sea breezes and limestone give structured, fresh, dark wines.
Which wines are based on Montepulciano?
Vino Nobile is Sangiovese from the Tuscan town.

Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is a deep cherry-pink rosé from Montepulciano, its own DOC since 2010. Cerasuolo means cherry-like. Short skin contact with this deeply coloured grape gives a darker, fuller rosé than most, with cherry, strawberry and a savoury edge.
Its deep cherry colour gives Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo its name.
Colline Teramane is Abruzzo's DOCG Montepulciano
Conero, by the sea, makes structured Montepulciano
Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is a deep cherry rosé

Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is a classic pizza and pasta wine: its soft tannins and dark fruit suit tomato sauce, sausages and grilled meat. In Abruzzo, it goes with arrosticini, lamb skewers. Cerasuolo suits fish soups, charcuterie and summer food.

Serve at 16 to 18 degrees; Cerasuolo chilled at 10 to 12. Simple Montepulciano is best within three years. Colline Teramane and Conero Riserva age 10 to 15 years; some traditional producers' wines last decades.
Simple wines young; the best for decades
Which dish is a classic Abruzzo partner for Montepulciano?
Grilled lamb skewers are Abruzzo's traditional match.
An everyday Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is one of Italy's best-value reds for pizza night.
Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is best served chilled.
Yes. As a rosé, it's served at 10 to 12 degrees.
